title: Share price numbers for the Hugging Face incident - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Following disclosure of the Hugging Face/OpenAI security incident, major publicly-traded cybersecurity firms lost $65-80 billion (8-10% of combined value) before recovering roughly $58 billion (70-90% of the drawdown) by early September; Cowen argues this modest, largely-recovered market reaction is evidence against claims that AI models pose imminent catastrophic risk.

themes.theme: Market-based measurement of the Hugging Face/OpenAI incident's fallout

insights.claim: Major publicly traded cybersecurity firms lost roughly $65-80 billion in combined market value, about 8-10% of their combined value, in the days following disclosure of the Hugging Face/OpenAI incident.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Gives a dollar-denominated, market-implied estimate of how much value investors assigned to prior cybersecurity protections being undermined by the incident — a reference point for pricing future AI-security shocks.
insights.quote: major publicly traded cybersecurity firms lost roughly $65–80 billion, or about 8–10% of their combined value, in the days following disclosure of the Hugging Face/OpenAI incident

insights.claim: By early September 2026, cybersecurity firms had recovered roughly $58 billion of the drawdown, representing about 70-90% of the initial loss, depending on whether July 15 or July 20 is used as the pre-event baseline.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A fast, near-complete recovery in cybersecurity equity values suggests the market treated the incident as a manageable, one-off shock rather than a signal of structural, ongoing AI-security failure.
insights.quote: by early September they had recovered roughly $58 billion, representing about 70–90% of that drawdown

insights.claim: Cowen argues that if AI models had truly been on the verge of doing catastrophic things, markets would likely have priced cybersecurity protection value falling by much more than 8-10%, so the actual, largely-reversed drawdown is evidence against the most severe AI-risk narratives.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Provides a falsifiable, market-based test for AI catastrophic-risk claims: track cybersecurity-sector valuations after future AI incidents as a real-time gauge of how seriously markets take escalating AI risk.
insights.quote: if the AI models were on the verge of doing truly terrible things to us, the market might estimate the value of our cyberprotection of falling more than eight to ten percent?

insights.claim: Cowen proposes using market prices — not the VIX, which he says is inadequate for this purpose — as a general discipline for evaluating AI-risk claims, arguing that people who dismiss market prices as too limited to capture AI risk should be asked whether they would in fact be alarmed and cite the numbers if the relevant companies' values fell by ninety percent.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A reusable heuristic for investors: challenge doom narratives by asking what market move would actually validate them, then track whether that move occurs — useful discipline for sizing AI-risk hedges rationally rather than emotionally.
insights.quote: Overall I am extremely skeptical of arguments that essentially take the form of "what I am concerned about is too big and too important to show up in any market prices."
